newsitem.title: UK: Sugar - Russia's import duty could hit Brazil raws.
newsitem.headline: Sugar - Russia's import duty could hit Brazil raws.

text.p: Brazilian sugar arriving in the Black Sea could be subject to Russia's 25 percent import tax for whites as its high purity level might not qualify it as raw sugar, brokers said on Thursday.
Brokers say Russia apparently expects significant quantities of Brazilian raws to arrive in the Black Sea, mainly as a result of the expiry of New York May futures.

London trade sources said a portion of Brazilian raw sugar now headed for Russia had a polarisation above 99.5 degrees, making it borderline material in terms of qualifying as raw and not white sugar.
Russia imposes a 25 percent duty on white sugar imports from all destinations except Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgystan, which have a customs treaty with Russia.
Polarisation, measured in degrees, gives an indication of the purity of the sugar. Unrefined raw sugar traditionally has a polarisation of 96 degrees.

"They (traders) are likely to face problems getting sugar of that sort of purity in as raw sugar," said one. "It could have all sorts of ramifications because not only are they taking it into Russia on their own account but they've also sold it to trade buyers."
Officials at Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossisk said one cargo of raws had been forced to pay extra duties by the customs services because the sugar it was carrying was at least partly refined.
"We have had a case where they started to offload a ship. However, the sugar was hardly raws but 90 percent refined, and they were made to pay an extra duty," the official was quoted as saying.

Other London traders said one possible solution would be to provide Russian customs with a bond to cover the added duty, which could then be returned after the seller had produced confirmation of refining.

The polarisation of bulk crystal sugar, while perhaps having a level of 99.5 degrees during loading, could often rise slightly during shipment and therefore account for the higher purity on later inspection, they said.
"They must be loading crystals or VHPs (very high polarity)...but that means that there is a big fat duty in Russia. If that's the case then they have a problem," said another trader.
"It's purely a commercial factor in relation to each country," he said.

Many countries will accept semi-finished raw sugar because it is cheaper to complete the refining process than buy whites. But others, such as Russia, want to protect their domestic industries and so impose a duty.
Trade sources in Russia have said raw sugar shipments would have to arrive by mid-July to be processed at domestic refineries before the Russian beet crop supplanted them as a feedstock.
Russian refineries needed between 14 and 21 days for processing and would be less keen to contract for raws as the beet harvest approached, they said.

At the expiry of the May New York raws contract, U.S. trade house Cargill took delivery of 260,000 long tons ex-Paranagua, widely believed by traders in Brazil and London to be new crop sugar and not stocks.
